analysis.one_liner: Requires tax-exempt hospitals to spend on charity care at least the value of their tax breaks.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee for the entire two-year Congress with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Nonprofit hospitals pay no federal, state, or local taxes in exchange for serving their communities. This bill would have forced them to spend, on patient care, training, and facilities, at least the full dollar value of the tax exemptions they receive each year. It would also bar hospitals from capping the number of Medicare and Medicaid patients they accept, cap the share of the requirement they can meet by buying up facilities, require them to bill uninsured patients who get financial help at Medicare rates rather than their inflated sticker prices, and order two government reviews of hospital financial-assistance policies and IRS enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients at tax-exempt hospitals, especially the uninsured and people on Medicare and Medicaid, who would get more free or discounted care, fairer bills, and assurance that hospitals receiving tax breaks accept public-insurance patients without limits.

how_it_helps.text: Nonprofit hospitals would have to spend at least the full value of their federal, state, and local tax exemptions each year on training, research, facility improvements, and free or discounted care.
Hospitals could not limit the number of Medicare or Medicaid patients they serve at any site they own or control, and their boards would have to be drawn from the local community.

Facility and equipment spending could count for no more than half the minimum requirement, and hospital acquisitions — such as buying physician practices — would not count at all, so the spending would have to reach actual patient care.
Financial assistance would have to be billed according to Medicare rates, stopping the practice of charging low-income patients the hospitals' full list prices.
The Treasury Inspector General would review hospitals' financial-assistance policies annually, and the Government Accountability Office would audit how well the IRS enforces the new standard.

analysis.who_pays: Tax-exempt hospital organizations, which would have to redirect money toward patient care and financial assistance, and could lose their tax-exempt status if they failed to meet the new standards.

drawbacks.text: The spending requirement counts training, education, research, and facility upgrades toward the minimum, so a hospital could comply by spending on buildings and equipment rather than on directly helping patients.
'A board of directors drawn from the community' is a vague standard that would leave the IRS broad discretion and could invite disputes over compliance.

Facing a spending requirement equal to their full tax benefit, some hospitals might convert to for-profit status instead of complying, which could leave patients without an obligation to provide community benefits at all.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's goal — making tax-exempt hospitals earn their tax breaks by treating Medicare, Medicaid, and low-income patients — is straightforward and would likely direct real resources toward patient care. Its main weaknesses are design: the spending definition is loose enough to reward facility spending, and the community-board standard is vague. On balance, the benefits to patients would probably outweigh the compliance burden, though hospitals could also respond by giving up their nonprofit status.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never moved further — no markup, no vote, and not a single cosponsor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Victoria Spartz (R-IN) introduced the bill on April 25, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
No one joined as a cosponsor — the cosponsor list shows zero members for the life of the bill.
The committee referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee on December 17, 2024, near the end of the two-year Congress, but the subcommittee never acted on it and it never received a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tax-exempt hospital systems, which keep their tax exemptions without facing new spending or patient-acceptance requirements. They are better off because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Rep. Victoria Spartz
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Ways and Means Committee.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the tax code
against.what_they_did: Sat on the bill for the full two-year Congress, finally referring it to a subcommittee in December 2024 without holding a markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: No bloc formed on either side: the bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so support was never partisan in shape — it was simply absent.

industries.note: The bill would have required them to spend at least the value of their tax exemptions on care, training, and facilities, barred limits on Medicare and Medicaid patients, and forced Medicare-rate billing for financial assistance. Because these hospitals' tax breaks are justified by community benefit, the bill's demands run alongside patients' interests, though hospitals would bear the direct cost.
